title: Project Azorian: The CIA's Super 70s Mission To Steal A Sunken Soviet Sub
summary: Hosts Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant cover Project Azorian, the 1970s CIA operation to recover the sunken Soviet Golf II submarine K-129 from the Pacific floor using the Hughes Glomar Explorer, a cover story built around Howard Hughes and deep-sea manganese mining. They describe the 1968 sinking, the US locating the wreck via hydrophone data, the engineering of the claw and recovery ship, the mission's partial success when the sub broke apart, the burial at sea of six Soviet sailors, the 1975 Hughes office break-in and blackmail attempt, the Los Angeles Times leak, and the origin of the "Glomar response." The episode ends with a listener mail about a charity Tribute night for brain cancer research.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts open with off-topic banter about Atlanta Time Machine, Waylon Jennings and Johnny Cash, and a tangent about Kissinger's teeth before previewing the CIA, submarine, and Howard Hughes story.

segments.title: Sinking of the Soviet sub K-129
segments.summary: A Soviet Golf II submarine, K-129, carrying nuclear missiles and nuclear torpedoes, sinks in the northwest Pacific in March 1968 after torpedo detonations; all crew are lost and the wreck lies about 16,500 feet down. The Soviets search for months without finding it.

segments.title: US locates the wreck and launches Project Azorian
segments.summary: US Navy and Air Force hydrophone data is combined to pinpoint the wreck. The Halibut submarine photographs it, and the CIA launches Project Azorian to attempt recovery for intelligence and warhead technology and cryptographic equipment.

segments.title: Engineering the recovery and the Glomar Explorer cover story
segments.summary: A secret working group designs the recovery method: a recovery ship with a moon pool and legs, a claw vehicle hidden inside a submersible barge, and Howard Hughes's Summa Corporation as contractor. The ship is called Hughes Glomar Explorer, with a cover story about deep-sea manganese nodule mining.

segments.title: Decision to proceed and mission departure
segments.summary: After years of delay, a second committee decides to proceed for intelligence and cryptographic reasons, and the Kissinger-era government worries about appearing wishy-washy to contractors. Planning includes provisions for handling Soviet remains under the Geneva Convention. The ship departs Los Angeles in June 1974 with an estimated high chance of success.

segments.title: Recovery operation and the sub breaking apart
segments.summary: The Glomar Explorer lowers the claw on pipe sections while Soviet ships shadow it. The claw grabs the sub and lifts it, but the hull breaks apart, dropping most of the wreck back to the seafloor; the forward section with some intelligence targets is recovered along with nuclear torpedoes and exposed crew, and six Soviet sailors' bodies are recovered and given a burial at sea.

segments.title: Aftermath, leak, and Glomar response
segments.summary: The CIA considers a second attempt, but Nixon's resignation and lack of value of codes end it. Seymour Hersh is pressured to hold a story; Harriet Phillippi's inquiry leads to the Glomar response phrase. A 1975 Hughes office break-in, a blackmail attempt, and an LA Times leak reveal the project; Jack Anderson publicizes it and the Soviets stay quiet.

segments.title: Costs, ship's fate, and speculation
segments.summary: The hosts note the project's cost around three billion in today's money, that the Glomar Explorer was later retrofitted for deep-sea drilling and sold for scrap about eight years earlier for fifteen million dollars, and discuss theories that the story is partly a cover story.

segments.title: Listener mail: Grace Giving charity
segments.summary: A listener promotes Grace Giving, a charity running a Tribute night for brain cancer research in Chicago, and the hosts encourage donations and provide contact info.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank listeners and point to the website and social accounts.
